title: Cap. IV Arg. 2 Sol: two pleasing — destined vs adopted; Orange 25; first love from God's fountain
pass_a_gloss: Further we rightly say that certain ones please God before others, as destined to faith and eternal life; certain ones also please God as sons of God already actually adopted, sanctified, and accepted to the right of eternal life. In the prior sense (which we ought to regard in this controversy) it is not only possible that someone please God before his faith had or foreseen, but plainly impossible that he please otherwise. Most well the Council of Orange, canon 25. Displeasing we were loved, that there might be made in us whence we might please. For if we could receive no benefit from God, unless we first pleased him, but we could not please, unless we first have faith: either we have the benefit of faith itself from ourselves, not from God, or a process into infinity will be given. One ought therefore to know that the reason of the first complacency, or of the Divine love toward the fallen creature, is not to be sought in some antecedent good quality of man, but is to be fetched from the very fountain of Divine love. For love is the first gift, in which all the rest are gifted: and the love of God has this singular, that it does not find but makes its object lovable to itself. Deut. 7:7, 8. The Lord your God chose you, that you might be to him a peculiar people, because the Lord loved you, not because you would surpass all nations in number.
pass_b_english: Further: some please God before others as destined to faith and eternal life; some please as sons already adopted, sanctified, and accepted to the right of eternal life. In the prior sense (ours in this controversy) it is not only possible that one please God before faith had or foreseen — it is plainly impossible to please otherwise. Best Orange canon 25: Displeasing we were loved, that there might be made in us whence we might please. If we could receive no gift from God unless we first pleased him, and could not please without faith first, then either faith's gift is from us not God, or you get an infinite regress. So the reason of first complacency — divine love toward the fallen creature — is not some antecedent good quality in man, but must be fetched from the fountain of divine love. Love is the first gift in which all others are given; and God's love has this singular: it does not find but makes its object lovable to itself (Deut. 7:7–8).
source_text: Porro recte dicimus quosdam placere Deo prae aliis, ut destinatos ad fidem et vitam aeternam; quosdam etiam placere Deo ut Dei filios actu jam adoptatos, sanctificatos, et ad jus vitae aeternae acceptatos. Priore sensu (quem nos respicere debemus in hac controversia) non modo possibile est ut quis ante habitam vel praevisam suam fidem placeat Deo, sed plane impossibile est ut aliter placeat. Optime Concilium Arausicanum, canone 25. Displicentes amati sumus, ut fieret in nobis unde placeremus. Si enim nullum beneficium a Deo accipere possemus, nisi prius ei placeremus, placere autem non possemus, nisi prius fidem habeamus: aut ipsum fidei beneficium a nobis, non a Deo habemus, aut dabitur processus in infinitum. Scire igitur oportet, rationem primæ complacentiae, sive amoris Divini erga lapsam creaturam, non in hominis bona aliqua qualitate antecedanea esse quaerendam, sed ex ipso fonte Divini amoris esse arcessendam. Nam amor est primum donum, in quo caetera omnia donantur: et amor Dei hoc habet singulare, quod non invenit sed facit suum objectum sibi amabile. Deut. vii. 7, 8. Te elegit Dominus Deus tuus, ut sis ei populus peculiaris, quia dilexit vos Dominus, non quia cunctas gentes numero vinceretis.
